messages.subject: Treatments spread over time
messages.body_plain:
Folks,

This is not a matchit question, but I wondered if I could access your wisdom.

Suppose there is a panel dataset, and different units get the
treatment at different dates. That is, there isn't a sharp date on
which the treatment is applied; different units get the treatment on
different dates.

We felt the right estimation strategy would be:

  1 Identify the units that never got treated; they're the control pool
  2 Walk through time. In each time period, identify the firms who are
treated. Find controls using propensity score matching where
information from that time period (only) is used. Once a control has
been used, flag it so it will never be used again.
  3 In this fashion, for each unit that's treated at time t, find a
control at that time t.
  4 Shift everything into event time where the treatment date is defined as 0
  5 Proceed with the analysis as usual.

Would appreciate your insights.

-- 
Ajay Shah

>> Suppose there is a panel dataset, and different units get the
>> treatment at different dates. That is, there isn't a sharp date on
>> which the treatment is applied; different units get the treatment on
>> different dates.
>>
>> We felt the right estimation strategy would be:
>>
>>  1 Identify the units that never got treated; they're the control pool
>>  2 Walk through time. In each time period, identify the firms who are
>> treated. Find controls using propensity score matching where
>> information from that time period (only) is used. Once a control has
>> been used, flag it so it will never be used again.
>>  3 In this fashion, for each unit that's treated at time t, find a
>> control at that time t.
>>  4 Shift everything into event time where the treatment date is defined as 0
>>  5 Proceed with the analysis as usual.

On Sat, Jan 14, 2012 at 8:01 PM, Kosuke Imai <kimai-uX/v2g6dJhCyum0STUha2w at public.gmane.org> wrote:
> That seems reasonable so long as the treatment is not given multiple times to each unit (in which case you probably need to match on the treatment history as well).

Thanks! Yes, we are being careful to screen the units. Only units that
never got treated are in the pool of controls and the units that got
treated exactly once are the treatment set. At the same time,
insisting on these features is hampering the size of the dataset.

Is there a literature on this kind of design that we should be looking at?

Elizabeth Stuart's 2010 survey article seems to suggest there are two
articles to look at, where individuals go in and out of the treatment
group : \textit{Marginal structural models and causal inference in
epidemiology}, by Robins, Hernan, Brumback, \textit{Epidemiology},
2000; and \textit{Balanced risk set matching}, by Li, Propert,
Rosenbaum, JASA, 2001.

-- 
Ajay Shah

messages.subject: Re: Treatments spread over time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ajay,
The articles you mention below are good places to start in terms of looking at similar examples to this.  The marginal structural models literature is for complex settings where you have time varying confounders and time varying treatments.   The balanced risk set matching reference might be particularly useful to you since I think it is a somewhat similar setting as yours-they essentially match on the hazard of starting treatment, matching people who are similar up to that point in time.

Others on the listserv might have other good references on this topic too.

Thanks,
Liz
